nameStory: The White M Hairstreak gets its name from the distinctive white 'M' marking on the underside of its hindwings, which stands out clearly against the darker background. Like other hairstreaks, it has delicate thread-like 'tails' extending from its hindwings that resemble fine hairs, giving this group of butterflies their charming common name.
description: The White M Hairstreak is a small, elegant butterfly with a wingspan of about 1.25 to 1.6 inches across. These gossamer-winged butterflies have dark wings that shimmer with an iridescent blue-green sheen near the base, especially noticeable in bright sunlight. The undersides are grayish-brown with the telltale white 'M' marking, while thin, hair-like tails dangle from the hindwings. Females are noticeably larger than males.

idTips.label: White M marking
idTips.description: Look for a bright white 'M' shape on the underside of the hindwings - it's crisp and unmistakable, like someone painted it with white correction fluid

idTips.label: Iridescent wing bases
idTips.description: The wing bases shimmer with blue-green iridescence that flashes and changes as the butterfly moves in sunlight, like oil on water

idTips.label: Hair-like tails
idTips.description: Delicate, thread-thin projections from the hindwings that flutter in the breeze and feel as fine as silk if you could touch them

idTips.label: Size difference by sex
idTips.description: Females are noticeably larger and more robust than the smaller, more delicate males when seen side by side

idTips.label: Grayish underside
idTips.description: The undersides appear muted gray-brown overall, providing perfect contrast for that bright white M to pop out

habitat: In New England, White M Hairstreaks are found in oak woodlands and forest edges, particularly where their host plants - various oak species - are abundant. Look for them in sunny clearings within oak forests, along woodland trails, and in areas where oaks meet open meadows or fields. They prefer areas with some elevation and well-drained soils where oaks thrive.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring, with fresh individuals appearing as oak leaves fully develop. This is when you'll see the most pristine specimens with bright white markings.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity occurs in summer when adults are most abundant and active, feeding on flower nectar and seeking mates around oak trees. Light green caterpillars can be found on oak leaves.
seasonality.fall: Adults may still be present in early fall, though they become less common and more worn-looking. Late-season individuals often show faded markings.
seasonality.winter: No adult activity - the species overwinters in the pupal stage, waiting for spring warmth to trigger emergence.

funFact: The White M Hairstreak's caterpillars are essentially living oak leaf decorations - they're perfectly camouflaged as light green miniature versions of the oak leaves they're munching on, making them nearly invisible even when feeding right out in the open.
confusionNotes: The white 'M' marking is so distinctive that this butterfly is rarely confused with other species once you see the underside. However, in flight or when wings are closed showing only the upper side, it might be mistaken for other small dark butterflies - always try to get a glimpse of those undersides for the telltale white M.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'hairstreaks,' these butterflies' wing tails aren't actually hair - they're modified wing scales that serve as false antennae to confuse predators about which end is the head, potentially allowing escape if attacked from behind.
compareHints: The White M Hairstreak is the only member of its genus found in New England, making it unique among our regional hairstreaks. Compared to other hairstreaks in our area like the Gray Hairstreak or Banded Hairstreak, the White M's distinctive bright white M-shaped marking on the hindwing underside is unmistakable and much more prominent than the subtle markings of its relatives.
